frames.narration: www.example.com has a failover record: server A is the primary and server B the secondary, with a TTL of 30 seconds. Health checkers in several regions probe A every 10 seconds, and the policy needs 3 failures in a row. The user's resolver has A cached.

Server A crashes. The next probe fails, and so does the one after it, but one or two failures are not enough: a single lost packet must not move all the traffic. The user's browser still gets A from the resolver's cache and sees errors.
The third failed probe, about 30 seconds after the crash, marks A unhealthy. The checkers send this to the change feed, and the feed delivers it to every site in a few seconds.
The site's policy table now returns B for www. New queries get the new answer, but the resolver still holds the old one for up to the rest of its 30-second TTL, so some users still reach A.
The resolver's cached entry expires. It asks the nearest anycast site for www again.
The site answers from memory in well under a millisecond of work: server B, TTL 30, signed with DNSSEC. The resolver validates the signature and caches B for another 30 seconds.

The user's next request goes to server B, which takes over. In total the user was affected for about 30 seconds of detection, a few seconds of publishing and up to 30 seconds of cache: about a minute. With a TTL of one hour the cache alone could have kept them on A for up to an hour.
